questions.questionText: Which of the following BEST describes the core principle behind the Agile Manifesto?

options.text: Comprehensive documentation over working software
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Following a plan over responding to change
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration

explanation.correct: The Agile Manifesto values individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change â€” placing these over processes, documentation, contracts, and plans.
explanation.incorrect: The Manifesto explicitly reverses these priorities â€” documentation, plans, and contracts are valued less than the items on the left side.
explanation.examTip: Agile Manifesto: 4 values, 12 principles. Values: Individuals > Processes, Working software > Docs, Customer collab > Contract, Responding to change > Plan.

questions.questionText: In Scrum, what is the purpose of a Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: To demonstrate completed work to stakeholders
To plan the work for the next sprint
To inspect the team process and identify improvements for the next sprint
To groom and prioritise the product backlog

explanation.correct: The Sprint Retrospective is a meeting where the team inspects how the last sprint went (processes, tools, relationships) and creates an improvement plan for the next sprint.
explanation.incorrect: Sprint Review = demo to stakeholders. Sprint Planning = plan next sprint work. Backlog Refinement = groom the backlog.
explanation.examTip: Scrum events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review (demo), Sprint Retrospective (improve). Retro = team improvement, Review = stakeholder demo.

questions.questionText: What are the three roles defined in the Scrum framework?

options.text: Project Manager, Developer, Tester
Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team
Business Analyst, Tech Lead, QA Engineer
Product Owner, Release Manager, Development Team

explanation.correct: Scrum defines exactly three roles: Product Owner (maximises value, owns backlog), Scrum Master (servant-leader, removes impediments), and Development Team (self-organising, cross-functional).
explanation.incorrect: Scrum has no Project Manager, Release Manager, Business Analyst, or separate Tester role. The Development Team is cross-functional and includes all skills needed.
explanation.examTip: No Project Manager in Scrum â€” that role is distributed. PO = what to build. SM = how the team works. Dev Team = builds it.

questions.questionText: Which Agile principle BEST describes the concept of delivering working software frequently?

options.text: Welcome changing requirements, even late in development
Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months
Build projects around motivated individuals
Simplicity is essential

explanation.correct: One of the 12 Agile principles explicitly states: 'Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter timescale.'
explanation.incorrect: The other options are also Agile principles but describe different concepts â€” change acceptance, motivated teams, and simplicity.
explanation.examTip: 12 Agile principles address: customer satisfaction, change, frequent delivery, collaboration, motivation, face-to-face, working software, sustainability, technical excellence, simplicity, self-organisation, reflection.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes Agile development concepts.

statements.text: In Kanban, work items are visualised on a board and WIP limits are used to control flow.
A Scrum Sprint always lasts exactly 4 weeks.
Extreme Programming (XP) includes practices such as pair programming and test-driven development.
The Product Backlog is owned and managed by the Scrum Master.

explanation.correct: Kanban uses WIP limits and visual boards. XP includes pair programming, TDD, continuous integration. The Product Backlog is owned by the Product Owner. Sprints are 1-4 weeks (timeboxed but not fixed at 4 weeks).
explanation.incorrect: Sprints can be 1-4 weeks. The Product Owner owns the backlog, not the Scrum Master.
explanation.examTip: Product Owner = owns and prioritises backlog. Scrum Master = facilitates and removes impediments. Dev Team = delivers.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a Definition of Done (DoD) in Agile?

options.text: To define the acceptance criteria for individual user stories
To provide a shared understanding of what 'complete' means for any increment of work
To document the release criteria for the final product
To specify the test cases that must pass before a story is accepted

explanation.correct: The Definition of Done is a shared checklist that every increment must meet to be considered complete â€” typically covering coding, testing, reviewing, and documentation standards.
explanation.incorrect: Acceptance criteria are story-specific. DoD applies to all stories. Release criteria may be separate. Test cases are part of DoD but not the whole definition.
explanation.examTip: DoD = team-level quality gate (applies to every story). Acceptance Criteria = story-specific business conditions. Both must be met.

questions.questionText: In Kanban, what is the purpose of a WIP (Work In Progress) limit?

options.text: To limit the number of team members working at any time
To control the amount of work in each stage to improve flow and identify bottlenecks
To restrict the number of user stories in the product backlog
To limit the number of sprints in a release

explanation.correct: WIP limits cap the number of items in each workflow stage, preventing overloading, exposing bottlenecks, and improving the overall flow of work through the system.
explanation.incorrect: WIP limits apply to work items, not people, backlogs, or sprints.
explanation.examTip: Kanban principles: visualise work, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively.

questions.scenarioText: A team has been using Scrum for 3 months. During retrospectives, they keep identifying the same impediment â€” the test environment is frequently unavailable during sprints. The Scrum Master has noted the impediment but no action has been taken.
questions.questionText: According to Agile principles, what should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: Remove the impediment from the retrospective notes as it is outside the team's control
Actively work to resolve the impediment, escalating to management if necessary
Add the impediment to the product backlog for the Product Owner to resolve
Ask the Development Team to work around the issue themselves

explanation.correct: The Scrum Master's primary responsibility is removing impediments to the Development Team's progress. When an impediment persists, the SM must escalate and actively resolve it.
explanation.incorrect: Ignoring, adding to the backlog (impediments are not product features), or delegating back to the team are all incorrect Scrum Master behaviours.
explanation.examTip: Scrum Master = servant leader and impediment remover. If the SM can't resolve it alone, they escalate to management or the organisation.

questions.questionText: What is the key difference between Agile and traditional (waterfall) development from a testing perspective?

options.text: In Agile, testing only happens at the end of the project
In Agile, testing is integrated throughout the development cycle rather than being a separate final phase
In Agile, testing is performed only by dedicated QA specialists
In Agile, there is no formal test documentation

explanation.correct: In Agile, testing is continuous and integrated â€” testers work alongside developers within each iteration. In waterfall, testing is typically a separate phase that occurs after development is complete.
explanation.incorrect: End-of-project testing is waterfall. Agile testing is shared responsibility. Agile has lightweight but still meaningful test documentation.
explanation.examTip: Agile testing = continuous, everyone's responsibility, integrated. Waterfall testing = separate phase, dedicated QA team, sequential.

questions.questionText: Which Agile framework focuses on visualising workflow, limiting work in progress, and managing flow rather than fixed-length iterations?

options.text: Scrum
Extreme Programming (XP)
Kanban
SAFe

explanation.correct: Kanban is a flow-based method that uses a visual board, WIP limits, and continuous flow â€” there are no sprints or iterations. Work is pulled when capacity is available.
explanation.incorrect: Scrum uses fixed sprints. XP uses iterations with specific engineering practices. SAFe scales Agile across large enterprises.
explanation.examTip: Scrum = timeboxed sprints. Kanban = continuous flow. XP = engineering practices (TDD, pair programming). Know when each is most applicable.

questions.questionText: What does 'inspect and adapt' mean in the context of Scrum?

options.text: The QA team inspects code and adapts the test plan accordingly
The team regularly examines progress and processes, then makes adjustments to improve
Management inspects team velocity and adapts resource allocation
The Product Owner inspects the increment and adapts the release plan

explanation.correct: 'Inspect and adapt' is a core Scrum principle where the team regularly examines their work, processes, and progress, then makes necessary adjustments â€” embodied in the Sprint Review and Retrospective.
explanation.incorrect: Inspect and adapt applies to the whole team and their processes, not just code inspection or management review.
explanation.examTip: Scrum pillars: Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation. All Scrum events are inspect-and-adapt opportunities.

questions.questionText: What is a user story in Agile development?

options.text: A detailed technical specification of a software feature
A short description of a feature from the perspective of the end user, capturing what they want and why
A log of bugs found during testing
A test case written in natural language

explanation.correct: A user story is a lightweight requirement expressed from the user's perspective: 'As a [user], I want [feature] so that [benefit].' It focuses on value, not technical implementation.
explanation.incorrect: Technical specs are too detailed for user stories. Bug logs are different. Test cases have a different format and purpose.
explanation.examTip: User story format: 'As a [persona], I want [goal], so that [reason].' Include acceptance criteria to define when the story is complete.

questions.questionText: What is the Agile Testing Quadrants model used for?

options.text: To define the roles of testers in an Agile team
To categorise tests by their purpose (supporting the team vs. critiquing the product) and their nature (business-facing vs. technology-facing)
To prioritise test cases in the regression suite
To define the four phases of Agile testing

explanation.correct: The Agile Testing Quadrants (Brian Marick) organise tests into 4 quadrants: Q1 (technology-facing, support team â€” unit/component tests), Q2 (business-facing, support team â€” functional/story tests), Q3 (business-facing, critique product â€” exploratory/usability), Q4 (technology-facing, critique product â€” performance/security).
explanation.incorrect: Quadrants are about test categories and purpose, not roles, regression prioritisation, or phases.
explanation.examTip: Q1=unit tests (automated), Q2=functional/story tests (automated+manual), Q3=exploratory/usability (manual), Q4=performance/security (tools). All quadrants needed.

questions.questionText: What does 'shift left' mean in the context of Agile testing?

options.text: Moving testers to sit on the left side of the development team
Performing testing activities earlier in the development lifecycle to find defects sooner
Reducing the number of test cases in the regression suite
Prioritising left-side quadrant tests over right-side quadrant tests

explanation.correct: Shift left means moving testing earlier in the SDLC â€” involving testers in requirements, writing tests before code (TDD), and running automated tests as part of development rather than waiting for a dedicated test phase.
explanation.incorrect: Shift left is a metaphor â€” the 'left' refers to earlier in the project timeline, not physical positioning or quadrant selection.
explanation.examTip: Shift left benefits: cheaper defect fixing, earlier feedback, better quality. Enables: TDD, BDD, continuous integration, early test design.

questions.questionText: In an Agile project, who is responsible for testing?

options.text: Only the dedicated QA testers on the team
The entire cross-functional team, including developers, testers, and the business
The Scrum Master, as they are responsible for quality
An external QA team that operates independently from the development team

explanation.correct: In Agile, quality and testing are a shared responsibility of the whole team â€” developers write unit tests, testers design and execute tests, and the business provides acceptance criteria and validates stories.
explanation.incorrect: Testing is not the sole responsibility of QA, the Scrum Master, or an external team. The whole team owns quality.
explanation.examTip: Agile testing mindset: whole team approach. Developers test their code. Testers work with developers. Business defines acceptance criteria.

questions.scenarioText: A tester joins an Agile team mid-project. During sprint planning, the team is estimating user stories. The tester notices several stories have no acceptance criteria.
questions.questionText: What should the tester do?

options.text: Accept the stories as-is and write test cases based on their own interpretation
Raise the concern and work with the team to define acceptance criteria before committing to the stories
Reject all stories without acceptance criteria from the sprint
Ask the Scrum Master to write the acceptance criteria

explanation.correct: Testers add value by raising quality concerns early. Stories without acceptance criteria are ambiguous and untestable â€” the tester should collaboratively work with the team to define them before sprint commitment.
explanation.incorrect: Working from assumptions risks building the wrong thing. Blanket rejection is too extreme. Writing criteria is a team activity, not the Scrum Master's job.
explanation.examTip: Tester value in sprint planning: ask testability questions, identify missing acceptance criteria, estimate test effort, and flag ambiguous stories.

questions.questionText: What is the primary purpose of test automation in Agile development?

options.text: To eliminate the need for manual testing entirely
To provide fast, repeatable feedback on whether recent changes have broken existing functionality
To replace exploratory testing with scripted test execution
To reduce the size of the development team

explanation.correct: Test automation in Agile primarily supports continuous integration by providing rapid feedback on regression â€” every code commit triggers automated tests that quickly identify if something is broken.
explanation.incorrect: Automation complements manual testing, doesn't replace it. Exploratory testing is still essential. Automation doesn't reduce headcount.
explanation.examTip: Automation in Agile: regression safety net, fast CI/CD feedback, enables frequent releases. Manual testing still needed for: exploratory, usability, new feature testing.

questions.questionText: What is a test pyramid and why is it important in Agile?

options.text: A model showing that more UI tests should be written than unit tests
A model that guides teams to write more low-level fast tests (unit) and fewer slow high-level tests (UI/E2E) for an efficient test suite
A hierarchy of who should write tests in an Agile team
A risk-based prioritisation model for test cases

explanation.correct: The test pyramid (Mike Cohn) shows: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and few slow UI/E2E tests at the top. This keeps the test suite fast and maintainable.
explanation.incorrect: The pyramid specifically advises FEWER UI tests, not more. It's about test distribution, not team hierarchy or risk prioritisation.
explanation.examTip: Test pyramid: Unit (many, fast, cheap) â†’ Integration (fewer) â†’ UI/E2E (few, slow, expensive). Avoid the 'ice cream cone' anti-pattern (inverted pyramid).

questions.questionText: What is exploratory testing and when is it particularly valuable in Agile?

options.text: Testing performed without any documentation to reduce overhead
Simultaneous test design, execution, and learning â€” particularly valuable for discovering unexpected defects in new features
Automated testing that explores all possible code paths
Testing performed only at the end of a sprint to validate new features

explanation.correct: Exploratory testing uses the tester's skill, curiosity, and knowledge simultaneously to design and execute tests. In Agile, it's valuable for investigating new features, edge cases, and areas automated tests miss.
explanation.incorrect: Exploratory testing is not undocumented â€” session-based notes are taken. It's not automated, and it's not restricted to end of sprint.
explanation.examTip: Exploratory testing: session-based, time-boxed, charter-driven. Complements scripted testing. Best for: new features, complex flows, usability issues.

questions.questionText: What is continuous integration (CI) and why does it benefit testing in Agile?

options.text: A practice of integrating all team members into a single open-plan office
A practice of frequently merging code changes into a shared repository and running automated tests to detect integration issues early
A process of integrating testing tools with development environments
A release process that integrates final testing with deployment

explanation.correct: CI involves developers frequently committing code to a shared repository, triggering automated builds and test suites. This catches integration defects early, provides rapid feedback, and keeps the codebase always releasable.
explanation.incorrect: CI is an engineering practice about code integration and automated testing, not office layout, tool integration, or the release process.
explanation.examTip: CI pipeline: commit â†’ build â†’ automated tests (unit, integration) â†’ report. Failing build = immediate fix required. Enables rapid feedback.

questions.questionText: How should testers handle regression testing in Agile when new functionality is added every sprint?

options.text: Perform full manual regression testing at the end of every sprint
Automate regression tests to run in the CI pipeline, supplemented by risk-based manual regression
Only test new functionality, as regression testing slows down the team
Outsource regression testing to a separate offshore QA team

explanation.correct: In Agile, automated regression tests integrated into CI provide fast, continuous regression coverage. Risk-based selection of manual regression tests ensures critical areas are covered without slowing delivery.
explanation.incorrect: Full manual regression each sprint is unsustainable. Skipping regression risks breaking existing functionality. Outsourcing breaks the whole-team principle.
explanation.examTip: Growing regression suite + short sprints = automation is essential. Automate stable tests. Use risk-based selection for manual regression. Refactor tests regularly.

questions.scenarioText: At the end of sprint 5, the team has accumulated 47 defects that were found but not fixed because they were deemed low priority. The Product Owner wants to focus only on new features in upcoming sprints.
questions.questionText: What risk does this situation represent and what should the team do?

options.text: No risk â€” low priority defects can always be fixed later before release
Technical debt risk â€” the team should allocate capacity to address defects alongside new features to prevent quality degradation
The Scrum Master should close all low-priority defects without fixing them
The team should stop all new feature development until defects are resolved

explanation.correct: Accumulating unfixed defects is technical debt that compounds over time â€” making future changes harder and increasing the risk of cascading failures. The team should regularly allocate sprint capacity to address defect debt.
explanation.incorrect: Deferring all defects is risky. Closing without fixing masks the problem. Stopping all features is too extreme. Balance is needed.
explanation.examTip: Technical debt in testing: unresolved defects, missing test coverage, manual processes that should be automated. Address continuously, not in a big-bang cleanup.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes testing in Agile projects.

statements.text: In Agile, testers should be involved from the first day of a sprint, including planning and refinement.
A Definition of Done that includes testing criteria helps ensure quality is built in rather than inspected in.
In Agile, test documentation is not required because the team relies on communication instead.
Pairing a tester with a developer during story implementation reduces defect injection.

explanation.correct: Testers should be involved from day 1 (sprint planning, refinement). DoD with test criteria ensures quality is built in. Tester-developer pairing reduces defects. Agile still requires lightweight but sufficient test documentation.
explanation.incorrect: Agile doesn't eliminate documentation â€” it eliminates unnecessary documentation. Test plans, results, and defect records are still needed.
explanation.examTip: Agile documentation: lightweight but sufficient. Test charters, session notes, defect logs, and automated test results are all valid Agile test artifacts.

questions.questionText: What is the main challenge for testers when requirements change frequently in Agile?

options.text: Testers cannot write any tests until requirements are finalised
Automated tests and test documentation must be updated to reflect requirement changes, risking test maintenance overhead
Frequent requirement changes eliminate the need for regression testing
Testers should refuse to test stories with changing requirements

explanation.correct: Frequent changes mean tests must be continuously maintained. Automated tests that are not updated become misleading (false passes/fails). Managing this test maintenance overhead is a key Agile tester challenge.
explanation.incorrect: Waiting for stable requirements is waterfall thinking. Changes increase regression testing need. Refusing to test is not a valid option.
explanation.examTip: Agile tester challenges: changing requirements, technical debt in tests, insufficient time for non-functional testing, team collaboration skills needed.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a sprint demo (Sprint Review) from a testing perspective?

options.text: To perform final acceptance testing of all sprint stories
To obtain stakeholder feedback on completed functionality, which can inform future testing priorities
To assign defects found by stakeholders to developers
To evaluate the team's testing process and identify improvements

explanation.correct: The Sprint Review gives stakeholders visibility into working software, and their feedback helps the team understand if the product meets expectations â€” informing backlog priorities and future test focus areas.
explanation.incorrect: Acceptance testing should happen within the sprint, not at the review. The review is not a defect assignment session. Process improvement is the Retrospective's purpose.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Review = stakeholder feedback on WHAT was built. Sprint Retrospective = team reflection on HOW they worked. Both valuable for testers.

questions.questionText: What is Test-Driven Development (TDD)?

options.text: Writing all test cases before the project starts and executing them at the end
A development practice where tests are written before the production code, guiding the design and implementation
A technique for driving the development team using test metrics
Running automated regression tests before deploying to production

explanation.correct: TDD follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle: write a failing test (Red), write minimal code to make it pass (Green), then refactor the code while keeping tests passing.
explanation.incorrect: TDD is a story-level micro-cycle, not a project-level activity. It's about developer workflow, not metrics or deployment gating.
explanation.examTip: TDD cycle: Red (write failing test) â†’ Green (write minimal code to pass) â†’ Refactor (clean up). Drives clean, testable design. Primarily unit test level.

questions.questionText: What is Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD)?

options.text: An extension of TDD where unit tests are used for acceptance testing
A collaborative practice where the whole team defines acceptance tests before development to create a shared understanding of requirements
A process where customers perform acceptance testing after every sprint
Automated deployment driven by acceptance test results

explanation.correct: ATDD involves business, developers, and testers collaboratively defining acceptance tests (in the form of examples or scenarios) before development begins â€” creating a shared understanding and executable specifications.
explanation.incorrect: ATDD is not unit testing. It involves the whole team, not just customers. It's not about deployment automation.
explanation.examTip: ATDD = collaborative requirements + acceptance tests before coding. BDD is an implementation of ATDD using Given/When/Then format. Both improve shared understanding.

questions.questionText: What is Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD) and what format are its scenarios written in?

options.text: A testing framework that focuses on the behaviour of individual code units; scenarios are written in programming language syntax
A collaborative development approach where scenarios are expressed in Given/When/Then format to describe expected system behaviour
A performance testing approach that describes user behaviour under load
A test management framework using case-based reasoning

explanation.correct: BDD extends ATDD by using a natural language format (Given/When/Then â€” Gherkin syntax) to describe system behaviour as executable specifications that all stakeholders can understand.
explanation.incorrect: BDD is not unit testing, performance testing, or case-based reasoning.
explanation.examTip: BDD format: Given [precondition], When [action], Then [expected outcome]. Tools: Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave. Creates living documentation.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of a BDD scenario written in correct Given/When/Then format?

options.text: Test: user_login. Steps: enter username, enter password, click login. Expected: dashboard displayed.
Given the user has valid credentials, When they submit the login form, Then they should be redirected to the dashboard.
As a user, I want to log in so that I can access my account.
Verify that login works with valid username and password.

explanation.correct: Option B correctly uses the Given (precondition), When (action/event), Then (expected outcome) BDD format for expressing system behaviour.
explanation.incorrect: Option A is a traditional test case format. Option C is a user story format. Option D is a vague test objective without Given/When/Then structure.
explanation.examTip: BDD = Given/When/Then. Multiple Whens and Thens use 'And'. Background = shared Given steps. Scenario Outline = parameterised scenarios.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between TDD, ATDD, and BDD?

options.text: They are three names for the same practice
TDD = developer unit tests; ATDD = team-defined acceptance tests; BDD = behaviour scenarios in natural language bridging business and technical perspectives
TDD = manual testing; ATDD = automated testing; BDD = performance testing
TDD is for testers, ATDD for business analysts, BDD for developers

explanation.correct: TDD focuses at the unit/code level (developer-facing). ATDD focuses at the story/acceptance level (whole team). BDD extends ATDD with natural language (Given/When/Then) to improve collaboration between business and technical team members.
explanation.incorrect: They are distinct practices at different levels. TDD is developer-focused, not tester-focused. None of them map to manual/automated/performance testing.
explanation.examTip: Progression: TDD (code level, developer) â†’ ATDD (story level, team) â†’ BDD (natural language, bridges business and tech). All support shift-left.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a task board (information radiator) in an Agile team?

options.text: To display the team's performance metrics to management
To provide the team with real-time, highly visible information about sprint progress and blockers
To track individual developer productivity
To replace all formal status reporting to stakeholders

explanation.correct: Information radiators (task boards, burndown charts) make work visible to the entire team â€” showing what's in progress, blocked, or done â€” enabling self-organisation and quick identification of issues.
explanation.incorrect: Task boards are for the team's benefit, not management surveillance or tracking individual productivity.
explanation.examTip: Information radiators: task board (stories/tasks), burndown chart (remaining work), test results dashboard. Visible to whole team and stakeholders.

questions.questionText: What does a burndown chart show in Agile?

options.text: The number of defects found per sprint over time
The remaining work versus time, showing progress toward completing the sprint or release goal
The team's velocity trend across sprints
The cost burn rate of the project against budget

explanation.correct: A burndown chart plots remaining work (story points or hours) against time. An ideal burndown line shows linear progress toward zero by the end of the sprint or release.
explanation.incorrect: Defect trends are shown in defect trend charts. Velocity is shown in velocity charts. Cost is shown in financial burndown charts â€” all different.
explanation.examTip: Sprint burndown: remaining story points per day. Flat line = blocked. Rising line = more work added. Steep drop = high productivity or over-estimation.

questions.scenarioText: A team is using BDD with Cucumber. During a three amigos meeting, the business analyst, developer, and tester are defining scenarios for a new payment feature. They discover that the feature behaves differently for premium vs standard accounts.
questions.questionText: What is the BEST way to capture this in BDD?

options.text: Write one generic scenario and add a comment explaining the difference
Write separate scenarios or use a Scenario Outline with an Examples table to cover both account types
Create a separate feature file for each account type
Add the account type difference to a test plan document instead

explanation.correct: A Scenario Outline with an Examples table is the BDD way to run the same scenario with different data (premium vs standard). This keeps scenarios DRY and makes the differences explicit and executable.
explanation.incorrect: Comments are not executable. Separate feature files are over-engineering. Test plan documents separate the specification from the executable tests.
explanation.examTip: Scenario Outline + Examples table = parameterised BDD tests. Each row in the Examples table creates a separate test run. Keeps scenarios concise.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a 'three amigos' meeting in Agile?

options.text: A daily standup for the three most senior team members
A short meeting between a business analyst, developer, and tester to clarify a story and define examples before development
A meeting between three Scrum teams to coordinate work
A retrospective format involving three rounds of feedback

explanation.correct: The three amigos meeting brings together the business (BA/PO), developer, and tester to discuss a story from three perspectives â€” ensuring shared understanding, surfacing edge cases, and defining examples before coding begins.
explanation.incorrect: It's a story-level collaboration meeting, not a daily standup, team coordination event, or retrospective format.
explanation.examTip: Three amigos = BA + Dev + Tester. Prevents misunderstandings. Produces examples that can become BDD scenarios or acceptance criteria.

questions.questionText: What is velocity in Agile and how is it useful for testing planning?

options.text: The speed at which individual developers write code
The average amount of work (story points) a team completes per sprint, used to forecast future sprint capacity
The number of test cases executed per day
A measure of how quickly defects are resolved

explanation.correct: Velocity measures how many story points a team completes per sprint on average. Testers can use velocity to plan testing capacity â€” estimating how much testing can realistically fit in upcoming sprints.
explanation.incorrect: Velocity is a team metric, not individual speed. It's not about test execution rate or defect resolution time.
explanation.examTip: Velocity = team capacity predictor. Used for release forecasting. New teams need 3-5 sprints to establish a stable velocity.

questions.questionText: What is the role of a tester in a DevOps/continuous delivery pipeline?

options.text: To perform manual testing gates before each deployment to production
To design, build, and maintain automated test suites that run as quality gates in the CI/CD pipeline
To manage the production deployment process
To approve changes to the production environment

explanation.correct: In DevOps, testers shift towards engineering â€” building automated test suites, defining quality gates in the pipeline, and collaborating on testing strategies that enable continuous, safe deployment.
explanation.incorrect: Manual gates slow down continuous delivery. Deployment management and change approvals are operational roles, not primary tester responsibilities.
explanation.examTip: DevOps tester: write automated tests, define pipeline quality gates, monitor production (testing in production), contribute to CI/CD pipeline design.

questions.questionText: What is a test charter in the context of session-based exploratory testing?

options.text: A legal document authorising the tester to access the system under test
A brief description of the mission, target area, and testing approach for a time-boxed exploratory testing session
A formal test plan signed off by the project manager
A list of all test cases to be executed in the sprint

explanation.correct: A test charter guides an exploratory testing session by defining: what area to explore, what to look for, and what approach to use â€” providing focus without scripting every step.
explanation.incorrect: Charters are lightweight, not legal documents or formal plans. They guide sessions, not replace scripted test lists.
explanation.examTip: Session-based testing: Charter (mission) + Time-box (60-90 min) + Session notes. Charters: 'Explore X using Y to discover Z.'

questions.questionText: How does Agile handle non-functional testing (performance, security, usability)?

options.text: Non-functional testing is postponed to a final hardening sprint before release
Non-functional requirements should be defined as acceptance criteria and tested incrementally throughout the project
Non-functional testing is the responsibility of a separate specialist team
Non-functional testing is not required in Agile projects as the focus is on working software

explanation.correct: In Agile, non-functional requirements (performance thresholds, security standards, accessibility) should be included in acceptance criteria and Definition of Done, and tested incrementally â€” not deferred to the end.
explanation.incorrect: Deferring all non-functional testing to the end is a common anti-pattern that leads to late discovery of fundamental architectural issues.
explanation.examTip: Non-functional requirements in Agile: include in DoD, define acceptance thresholds, test each sprint. Performance baseline early â€” regressions compound over time.

questions.questionText: What does 'test first' mean in Agile development?

options.text: Running all tests before writing any code
Writing automated tests or acceptance criteria before writing the production code they verify
Prioritising testing tasks over development tasks in the sprint
Testing in production before releasing to all users

explanation.correct: Test first means writing the test/acceptance criteria before the code â€” as in TDD (write failing test, then code) or ATDD (define acceptance tests before development). It drives design and prevents misunderstanding.
explanation.incorrect: Test first is a workflow principle, not a project sequencing rule. It's not about sprint priorities or production testing strategies.
explanation.examTip: Test first = TDD at unit level, ATDD at story level. Both ensure testability and clear requirements before coding begins.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes Agile testing methods and tools.

statements.text: A test automation framework should be maintained like production code â€” reviewed, refactored, and kept up to date.
BDD scenarios should be written by the tester alone to ensure technical accuracy.
Pair testing (a developer and tester working together) can improve code quality and test coverage.
Once a test is automated, it never needs to be reviewed or updated.

explanation.correct: Test automation code requires maintenance like production code. BDD scenarios should be written collaboratively (three amigos). Pair testing improves quality. Automated tests must be updated when requirements change.
explanation.incorrect: BDD is collaborative by definition. Automated tests become outdated and must be maintained as the product evolves.
explanation.examTip: Test automation debt: outdated tests, brittle tests, slow tests. Regular refactoring of the test suite is as important as maintaining production code.

questions.questionText: What is the tester's role during backlog refinement in Scrum?

options.text: Testers do not participate in backlog refinement
Testers help clarify acceptance criteria, identify testability issues, and estimate testing effort for backlog items
Testers are only responsible for re-ordering the backlog by risk
Testers write all the acceptance criteria for each backlog item

explanation.correct: During refinement, testers add value by asking clarifying questions, identifying ambiguous or untestable requirements, flagging missing acceptance criteria, and contributing to effort estimates for testing activities.
explanation.incorrect: Testers absolutely participate in refinement. They're not solely responsible for acceptance criteria (that's collaborative) or backlog ordering.
explanation.examTip: Tester questions during refinement: How will this be tested? What are the edge cases? What does done look like? Are there non-functional requirements?

questions.scenarioText: A tester estimates that a user story will require 3 days of testing work, but the team has only given 1 day of testing in the sprint. The developer says 'It's a small change, it won't need much testing.'
questions.questionText: What should the tester do?

options.text: Accept the estimate and complete what testing is possible in 1 day
Explain the testing scope and risks to the team and negotiate the estimate or story scope during sprint planning
Skip the story in this sprint and ask for it to be moved to the next sprint
Complete the story and mark it done regardless of testing coverage

explanation.correct: The tester must advocate for adequate testing time by clearly explaining what testing is required, what risks exist if it's reduced, and either negotiating the estimate or reducing the story scope to fit.
explanation.incorrect: Silently accepting insufficient time, skipping the story, or marking it done without proper testing are all quality risks the tester must flag.
explanation.examTip: Tester as quality advocate: speak up when testing is underestimated. Use risk language: 'If we only test for 1 day, we risk missing X, Y, Z edge cases.'

questions.questionText: What is a spike in Agile development?

options.text: A sudden increase in the number of defects reported
A time-boxed investigation to reduce uncertainty in a technical or business problem before committing to a solution
An emergency sprint to fix critical production defects
A type of performance test that simulates sudden traffic spikes

explanation.correct: A spike is a timeboxed research or prototyping activity used to gain knowledge needed to estimate or plan future work â€” reducing uncertainty before committing to a full implementation.
explanation.incorrect: A spike is about learning, not defect response, emergency sprints, or performance testing.
explanation.examTip: Technical spike = research a technology approach. Functional spike = prototype a feature concept. Output = knowledge/recommendation, not shippable product.

questions.questionText: What is the benefit of testers and developers sitting together (co-location) in an Agile team?

options.text: It ensures that testers can monitor developers to prevent defects being introduced
It enables faster communication, immediate defect discussion, and shared understanding of requirements
It allows the team to share a single computer
It makes it easier for the manager to observe the team's progress

explanation.correct: Co-location improves collaboration â€” testers can immediately raise questions with developers, defects can be fixed in minutes rather than days, and shared understanding prevents misinterpretation of requirements.
explanation.incorrect: Co-location is about collaboration and communication, not monitoring, equipment sharing, or management visibility.
explanation.examTip: Agile Manifesto: 'The most efficient and effective method of conveying information is face-to-face conversation.' Co-location or good collaboration tools support this.

questions.questionText: Place the TDD (Test-Driven Development) cycle steps in the correct order.

orderItems.text: Write a failing test for the new functionality (Red)
Write the minimal production code to make the test pass (Green)
Refactor the code while keeping all tests passing
Repeat for the next piece of functionality

explanation.correct: TDD Red-Green-Refactor: write failing test first (Red), implement minimal code to pass (Green), clean up the code (Refactor), then repeat.
explanation.incorrect: Writing code before the test defeats the purpose of TDD â€” the test must drive the implementation.
explanation.examTip: Red = test fails (expected â€” no code yet). Green = test passes (minimal code). Refactor = improve code quality. Never skip refactor.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between functional and non-functional testing in the context of Agile user stories?

options.text: Functional testing verifies the user story acceptance criteria; non-functional testing verifies quality attributes like performance, security, and usability
Functional testing is automated; non-functional testing is always manual
Non-functional testing replaces functional testing in Agile
Functional testing is done by the team; non-functional testing is done by external specialists only

explanation.correct: Functional tests verify WHAT the system does (business requirements, acceptance criteria). Non-functional tests verify HOW WELL it does it (performance thresholds, security compliance, usability standards).
explanation.incorrect: Both can be automated or manual. Non-functional complements functional. Both are the team's responsibility.
explanation.examTip: Include non-functional acceptance criteria in user stories: 'The page must load in under 2 seconds' or 'The login must pass OWASP Top 10 checks'.

questions.questionText: What does INVEST stand for in the context of user stories?

options.text: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Iterative, Necessary, Verified, Efficient, Scheduled, Tested
Incremental, New, Valuable, Executable, Stable, Tracked
Integrated, Noted, Verifiable, Essential, Simple, Transparent

explanation.correct: INVEST is a quality checklist for user stories: Independent (can be developed independently), Negotiable (not a contract), Valuable (delivers value), Estimable (can be estimated), Small (fits in a sprint), Testable (clear acceptance criteria).
explanation.incorrect: Only option A correctly spells out the INVEST acronym.
explanation.examTip: INVEST checklist: I-N-V-E-S-T. If a story isn't testable, it can't be accepted. If it's not small, it should be split. If not independent, scheduling becomes complex.

questions.scenarioText: A tester notices that the automated test suite takes 45 minutes to run, which blocks the CI pipeline and discourages developers from committing frequently.
questions.questionText: What strategy should the team adopt?

options.text: Remove all slow tests to reduce the suite to under 5 minutes
Implement a test pipeline with fast tests running first (unit/integration) and slow tests running in a separate stage or off the critical path
Accept the 45-minute build time as it ensures thorough testing
Move all tests to run nightly instead of on every commit

explanation.correct: A staged test pipeline runs fast tests (unit, fast integration) immediately on commit for rapid feedback, and slower tests (E2E, performance) in later stages â€” balancing speed with thoroughness.
explanation.incorrect: Removing slow tests loses coverage. 45 minutes blocks CI effectiveness. Nightly builds mean defects sit for hours before detection.
explanation.examTip: CI pipeline stages: commit stage (unit tests, < 5 min) â†’ acceptance stage (integration, E2E) â†’ exploratory/performance. Fast feedback on most common failures.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a retrospective action item from a testing improvement perspective?

options.text: To document what testing was completed in the sprint for the project record
To commit to a specific, measurable improvement to the testing process that the team will implement in the next sprint
To assign blame for testing failures in the previous sprint
To list all defects found in the sprint for management review

explanation.correct: Retrospective action items are concrete commitments to improve â€” for testing this might be: automate a specific regression test, add missing test environment, or implement a new testing technique.
explanation.incorrect: Retrospectives are forward-looking improvements, not documentation, blame, or defect reporting sessions.
explanation.examTip: Effective retro actions: specific, assigned to someone, timeboxed, and reviewed at the next retro. Avoid generic actions like 'improve communication'.

questions.questionText: What does 'done' mean for a user story according to the Definition of Done?

options.text: The developer has merged the code to the main branch
All DoD criteria are met â€” code complete, unit tested, reviewed, integration tested, acceptance criteria passed, and documentation updated
The story has been demonstrated to the Product Owner in the sprint review
The story has been deployed to production

explanation.correct: Done means ALL criteria in the Definition of Done are satisfied â€” this typically includes: code written and reviewed, unit tests passing, integration tests passing, acceptance criteria verified, DoD checklist complete.
explanation.incorrect: Code merge alone is not done. Sprint review demo is after done. Not all stories need to go to production at end of every sprint (though the increment should be releasable).
explanation.examTip: DoD creates a consistent quality bar. If a team has different DoDs per story, quality becomes inconsistent. DoD applies to every story.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a Definition of Ready (DoR) in Agile?

options.text: To define when the sprint is ready to end
To define the criteria a user story must meet before the team can commit to it in sprint planning
To describe when the product is ready for release to production
To define when testers are ready to start executing test cases

explanation.correct: The Definition of Ready is a checklist of conditions a backlog item must meet before the team commits to it in sprint planning â€” typically: story is written, acceptance criteria defined, dependencies identified, and it's estimable.
explanation.incorrect: DoR is about story readiness for sprint commitment, not sprint end, product release, or tester readiness.
explanation.examTip: DoR = story must meet this before pulling into sprint. DoD = story must meet this before calling it complete. Both prevent quality issues.

questions.questionText: How does risk-based testing apply in Agile?

options.text: Risk assessment is done once at the start of the project and never revisited
Risks are assessed at the start of each sprint to prioritise testing effort on the most critical and risky areas
Risk-based testing only applies to performance testing in Agile
Testers avoid risky areas to prevent finding too many defects

explanation.correct: In Agile, risk assessment is lightweight and iterative â€” done at sprint planning to focus testing effort where risk is highest. Risks change as the product evolves, so assessment is repeated each sprint.
explanation.incorrect: One-time risk assessment is waterfall thinking. Risk applies to all testing types. Testers should focus MORE on risky areas, not avoid them.
explanation.examTip: Agile risk-based testing: identify product risks per sprint, allocate more testing effort to high-risk stories, and adjust as new risks emerge.

questions.questionText: What is the daily standup (Daily Scrum) in Scrum?

options.text: A one-hour status meeting led by the project manager
A 15-minute time-boxed daily meeting where the team synchronises activity and identifies blockers
A daily code review session led by the tech lead
A meeting to report sprint progress to management

explanation.correct: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute time-boxed event for the Development Team to synchronise, plan the next 24 hours, and identify impediments. It is not a status report to management.
explanation.incorrect: No project manager leads the Daily Scrum. It's not a code review or management report. It's strictly time-boxed to 15 minutes.
explanation.examTip: Daily Scrum: What did I do yesterday? What will I do today? Any blockers? Scrum Master facilitates but doesn't own it. Keep to 15 minutes strictly.

questions.scenarioText: A team's automated test suite has a 15% false failure rate â€” 15% of test failures are not caused by actual defects but by test environment instability, timing issues, or flaky tests.
questions.questionText: What is the risk of a high false failure rate and what should the team do?

options.text: No risk â€” false failures are expected and can be ignored
It erodes trust in the test suite, causing developers to ignore failures. The team should investigate and fix flaky tests as a priority.
Add more tests to compensate for the false failures
Remove the failing tests from the CI pipeline until the environment is stable

explanation.correct: Flaky tests erode trust â€” when developers see failures they assume are false, they stop taking failures seriously and real defects get ignored. Fixing or quarantining flaky tests is critical to maintaining pipeline credibility.
explanation.incorrect: False failures cannot be ignored. More tests worsen the problem. Removing failing tests hides the issue and reduces coverage.
explanation.examTip: Flaky test management: quarantine flaky tests, investigate root cause (timing, environment, data), fix or delete them. Pipeline credibility depends on reliable results.

questions.questionText: What is the concept of 'built-in quality' in Agile?

options.text: Quality assurance is performed by a dedicated QA team at the end of development
Quality is incorporated throughout development through practices like TDD, code reviews, pairing, and continuous integration
The system is built with high-quality hardware components
Quality standards are built into the project contract

explanation.correct: Built-in quality means preventing defects rather than detecting them later â€” using practices like TDD, pair programming, code reviews, and CI to catch issues at the point of creation.
explanation.incorrect: Built-in quality is the opposite of end-stage QA. It's about process and engineering practices, not hardware or contracts.
explanation.examTip: Built-in quality: TDD + pair programming + code review + CI = fewer defects reaching testing. Prevention > Detection > Correction.

questions.questionText: Which tool category is most commonly used to support BDD in automated testing?

options.text: Load testing tools (e.g., JMeter, Gatling)
Behaviour specification frameworks (e.g., Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave)
Static analysis tools (e.g., SonarQube)
Test case management tools (e.g., TestRail)

explanation.correct: BDD frameworks like Cucumber (Java/Ruby), SpecFlow (.NET), and Behave (Python) parse Gherkin Given/When/Then scenarios and execute them as automated tests, linking business language to code.
explanation.incorrect: JMeter = performance. SonarQube = static code analysis. TestRail = test management. None support Given/When/Then scenario automation.
explanation.examTip: BDD tools: Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave, JBehave. Use Gherkin syntax. Scenarios become living documentation that's also executable.

questions.scenarioText: An Agile team has been delivering sprints for 6 months. A business stakeholder complains that while individual features work, the system as a whole is unreliable â€” components that worked before break when new features are added.
questions.questionText: What is the most likely root cause and how should the team address it?

options.text: The team is delivering too many features per sprint
Insufficient regression test coverage and integration testing between components
The Product Owner is prioritising the wrong stories
The Development Team needs to work longer hours to improve quality

explanation.correct: When new features break existing functionality, it signals inadequate regression coverage and integration testing. The team should invest in automated regression tests and integration testing to catch cross-component breakage.
explanation.incorrect: Feature volume, story prioritisation, or working hours are not the root cause. The systemic issue is a gap in the regression safety net.
explanation.examTip: Symptoms of poor regression coverage: 'works on my machine', passing unit tests but broken integrated system, increasing production defects over time.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of story points in Agile estimation?

options.text: To measure the exact number of hours a story will take to complete
To estimate the relative effort, complexity, and uncertainty of a user story compared to other stories
To track the number of test cases written for each story
To score the business value of each story for prioritisation

explanation.correct: Story points are a relative measure of size/effort/complexity â€” not absolute time. They allow teams to estimate without committing to specific hours and improve through calibration over multiple sprints.
explanation.incorrect: Story points are not hours, test counts, or business value scores (though value is a separate consideration for prioritisation).
explanation.examTip: Story points: relative sizing using Fibonacci (1,2,3,5,8,13,21...). 1 point = simplest story. Larger = more complex/unknown. Team consensus via planning poker.

questions.questionText: What is 'testing in production' and when might it be appropriate in Agile?

options.text: Testing performed by end users who discover bugs naturally
Deliberate strategies like A/B testing, canary releases, and feature flags that validate behaviour with real users in the production environment
Skipping test environments and deploying directly to production to save time
Having the QA team work in the production environment to test

explanation.correct: Testing in production includes deliberate techniques: A/B testing (compare variants), canary releases (gradual rollout), feature flags (selective enablement), and monitoring/observability â€” all used to validate real-world behaviour safely.
explanation.incorrect: Testing in production is a deliberate strategy, not accidental, a shortcut, or physical access to production servers.
explanation.examTip: Testing in production techniques: A/B testing, canary deployment, blue-green deployment, chaos engineering, synthetic monitoring. All require good observability.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes Scrum concepts.

statements.text: The Sprint Goal is set during Sprint Planning and provides focus for the sprint.
The Scrum Master has the authority to remove items from the Product Backlog.
The Sprint Backlog is owned by the Development Team and can be updated throughout the sprint.
In Scrum, a sprint can be cancelled by the Scrum Master if progress is too slow.

explanation.correct: Sprint Goal is set in planning. Sprint Backlog is owned and managed by Dev Team. Only the Product Owner can remove backlog items. Only the Product Owner can cancel a sprint (rarely done).
explanation.incorrect: Scrum Master does not own the backlog. Only the Product Owner can cancel a sprint â€” and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
explanation.examTip: PO owns: Product Backlog, Sprint Goal alignment, sprint cancellation. Dev Team owns: Sprint Backlog, technical decisions. SM owns: process facilitation.

questions.questionText: What is pair testing and what are its benefits?

options.text: Two testers independently testing the same feature and comparing results
A tester and developer working together at one workstation to test and debug simultaneously
Testers testing in pairs to reduce fatigue during long test sessions
Pairing a manual tester with an automation engineer to write test scripts

explanation.correct: Pair testing has a tester and developer collaborating at one workstation â€” the developer understands the code, the tester brings test design skills. Together they find defects faster and build shared quality understanding.
explanation.incorrect: Pair testing is collaborative, not independent parallel testing, fatigue management, or scripting partnership.
explanation.examTip: Pair testing benefits: immediate defect discussion, shared understanding, developer learns testing mindset, tester learns system internals. Reduces defect escape rate.

questions.questionText: What does 'living documentation' mean in the context of BDD?

options.text: Documentation that is updated manually by the technical writer after each sprint
Executable BDD scenarios that serve as both automated tests and always up-to-date specification documentation
An online wiki that the team updates after each release
A living document approach where requirements evolve with user feedback

explanation.correct: In BDD, Given/When/Then scenarios are both executable tests and specifications. When the tests pass, the documentation is accurate. They are 'living' because they automatically stay in sync with the system behaviour.
explanation.incorrect: Living documentation in BDD context is about executable specifications, not manually maintained wikis or requirements evolution.
explanation.examTip: BDD living documentation: scenarios = specs = tests. Tools like Cucumber + Serenity generate HTML reports showing which scenarios pass â€” always accurate documentation.

questions.questionText: What is the test strategy in an Agile project and how does it differ from traditional projects?

options.text: Agile projects do not have a test strategy â€” testing is ad-hoc
Agile test strategy is lightweight, evolves iteratively, and focuses on how the team will achieve quality goals rather than being a large upfront document
The test strategy is a fixed contract agreed with the customer before development starts
In Agile, the test strategy replaces the need for test cases

explanation.correct: Agile test strategy is typically a concise, living document defining testing approaches, tools, automation strategy, and quality goals â€” created early but updated as the project evolves. It's not eliminated, just lightened.
explanation.incorrect: Agile has test strategy but it's lighter than waterfall's comprehensive plans. It's not fixed upfront or a replacement for test cases.
explanation.examTip: Agile test strategy covers: test levels, techniques, tools, automation approach, environments, entry/exit criteria. Keep it concise and update each sprint.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a test coverage metric in Agile?

options.text: To guarantee that the software has no defects
To indicate how much of the code, requirements, or risk areas are exercised by tests, helping the team identify gaps
To measure individual tester productivity
To determine whether a story can be marked as done

explanation.correct: Test coverage metrics (code coverage, requirements coverage, risk coverage) help identify untested areas â€” not to guarantee quality, but to inform risk decisions about what has and hasn't been tested.
explanation.incorrect: 100% coverage doesn't guarantee no defects. Coverage is a team metric, not individual. DoD determines done status.
explanation.examTip: Coverage types: code coverage (% of code executed), requirements coverage (% of requirements tested), risk coverage (% of risk areas addressed). All have limitations.

questions.scenarioText: A tester is working on a feature that integrates with a third-party payment API. The API is not yet available in the test environment, blocking testing.
questions.questionText: What technique should the tester use to unblock testing?

options.text: Wait until the API is available before writing any tests
Use a test double (mock or stub) to simulate the API responses and continue testing
Mark the story as done and test the API integration in the next sprint
Remove the story from the sprint as it cannot be tested

explanation.correct: Test doubles (mocks, stubs, fakes) simulate external dependencies, allowing testing to proceed without the actual API. The mock can simulate both success and error responses to test all paths.
explanation.incorrect: Waiting, deferring, or removing the story are all avoidable if test doubles are used. This is a standard Agile testing technique for handling external dependencies.
explanation.examTip: Test doubles: Mock (verifies interactions), Stub (provides canned responses), Fake (lightweight working implementation), Spy (records calls). Use for external dependencies.

questions.questionText: What is the role of the Product Owner in relation to testing?

options.text: The Product Owner performs all user acceptance testing
The Product Owner defines acceptance criteria, reviews demos, and accepts or rejects completed stories based on whether they meet the acceptance criteria
The Product Owner writes automated acceptance tests
The Product Owner has no testing responsibilities â€” that belongs to the Development Team

explanation.correct: The Product Owner owns the acceptance criteria that define when a story is done from a business perspective. They review demos at the Sprint Review and provide feedback on whether stories meet business needs.
explanation.incorrect: PO typically doesn't write automated tests. UAT may involve the PO but the whole team is responsible for testing. PO has critical testing responsibilities.
explanation.examTip: PO testing role: define acceptance criteria, participate in story reviews, accept/reject stories at Sprint Review. Clear AC = testable stories.

questions.questionText: What is continuous testing in a DevOps context?

options.text: Having a tester continuously clicking through the application all day
The practice of running automated tests at every stage of the software delivery pipeline to provide immediate risk feedback
Writing new test cases continuously throughout the sprint
Continuously improving the test strategy document

explanation.correct: Continuous testing runs automated tests at every pipeline stage â€” from unit tests on commit, through integration and acceptance tests, to performance and security tests â€” providing risk assessment at each stage.
explanation.incorrect: Continuous testing is about automated pipeline execution, not manual clicking, test writing, or documentation improvement.
explanation.examTip: Continuous testing enables continuous delivery. Each pipeline stage provides a quality gate. Failed gate = fix before progressing, not skip and continue.

questions.questionText: What is the 'testing debt' concept in Agile?

options.text: The cost of buying testing tools and infrastructure
The accumulated backlog of testing work that was skipped or deferred â€” including missing tests, unautomated regression tests, and unresolved defects
The time owed to testers for overtime worked during sprints
The technical debt created by poor-quality test code

explanation.correct: Testing debt is the accumulated shortfall in testing â€” skipped tests, manual regression that should be automated, and deferred defects. Like technical debt, it compounds and increases risk over time.
explanation.incorrect: Testing debt is about missing testing coverage and deferred testing work, not costs, overtime, or code quality (that's technical debt in tests).
explanation.examTip: Address testing debt incrementally each sprint â€” don't let it accumulate. Common items: automate a set of manual regression tests, fix flaky tests, address deferred defects.

questions.questionText: What is a product increment in Scrum?

options.text: A list of all features added to the product backlog in a sprint
The sum of all completed backlog items at the end of a sprint that is in a potentially shippable state
A minor version release of the software
The set of user stories planned for the current sprint

explanation.correct: The Increment is the sum of all Product Backlog items completed during a sprint plus all previous sprints' increments â€” it must be in a usable, potentially releasable state regardless of whether it is released.
explanation.incorrect: The increment is about completed, working software â€” not backlog additions, version releases, or sprint plan items.
explanation.examTip: Increment = all done stories from this sprint + all previous sprints. Must meet DoD. Must be potentially releasable â€” even if not actually released.

questions.scenarioText: A tester joins a mature Agile team as the first dedicated tester. The team currently has no automated tests and relies on manual testing at the end of each sprint, which often results in carryover stories.
questions.questionText: What should the tester prioritise in the first few sprints?

options.text: Write 100% automated test coverage for all existing features immediately
Establish a test automation foundation starting with the most critical user journeys, while coaching developers on writing unit tests
Reject all sprint stories until proper test documentation is in place
Focus only on manual testing and report defects without changing team practices

explanation.correct: Building automation from the ground up requires prioritisation. Start with high-value, high-risk user journeys for E2E tests, encourage developers to add unit tests for new code, and build incrementally rather than trying to automate everything at once.
explanation.incorrect: 100% coverage immediately is unrealistic. Rejecting stories is too disruptive. Maintaining the status quo doesn't improve quality.
explanation.examTip: Introducing testing to a team: start with the most critical paths, build automation incrementally, coach developers, and make quality improvements visible to the team.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes test automation best practices in Agile.

statements.text: Automated tests should be independent of each other to prevent cascading failures.
UI-level automated tests are the most efficient type because they test the complete system.
Test data management is a critical part of maintaining a reliable automated test suite.
The goal of automation should be to replace all manual testing within 6 months.

explanation.correct: Independent tests prevent cascading failures. Test data management prevents flakiness. UI tests are the least efficient (slow, brittle) â€” unit tests are most efficient. Automation complements, not replaces, manual testing â€” no fixed timeline.
explanation.incorrect: UI tests are valuable but not the most efficient â€” they're slowest and most brittle. Automation doesn't replace all manual testing.
explanation.examTip: Automation best practices: independent tests, manage test data, mock external dependencies, favour unit over UI tests for speed, maintain like production code.

questions.questionText: What is the concept of 'sustainable pace' in Agile?

options.text: Delivering the maximum amount of features possible in every sprint regardless of team capacity
Working at a pace that the team can maintain indefinitely without burning out, ensuring consistent long-term quality and delivery
Slowing down delivery to ensure thorough documentation is produced
Delivering the same number of story points every sprint

explanation.correct: The Agile principle of sustainable pace means the team works at a consistent, manageable rate â€” overtime and crunch are red flags that indicate process problems, not badges of honour.
explanation.incorrect: Maximising output without regard for sustainability leads to burnout and quality decline. Sustainable pace is not about slowing down or fixed velocity.
explanation.examTip: Agile principle: 'The sponsors, developers, and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.' Overtime = process failure, not success.

questions.questionText: What is a test environment in Agile and what challenges can arise with it?

options.text: The physical location where testers sit in an Agile team
The configured infrastructure (hardware, software, data, configuration) required to run tests, which in Agile must be available frequently and reflect production closely
The online tool used to manage test cases and defects
The team agreement on how testing will be performed

explanation.correct: Test environments must be stable, available, and production-like for reliable test results. Agile challenges: shared environments causing conflicts, environment unavailability blocking testing, configuration drift from production.
explanation.incorrect: Test environments are infrastructure, not seating arrangements, tools, or agreements.
explanation.examTip: Agile environment challenges: environment availability, environment stability, test data management, configuration management. Solutions: dedicated environments, containerisation, IaC.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a sprint testing board separate from the team's main task board?

options.text: To keep testers' work hidden from developers
To provide testers with their own workflow visibility showing stories ready for test, in test, blocked, and done
To track defects found in previous sprints
To replace the main team board for testing activities

explanation.correct: A testing board or testing swimlane gives testers visibility into their specific workflow, helping them manage their work in progress, identify bottlenecks, and communicate testing status transparently to the team.
explanation.incorrect: The testing board is visible to the whole team. It's for workflow management, not defect tracking or replacement of the main board.
explanation.examTip: Testing workflow states: Story Ready for Test â†’ In Test â†’ Defects Raised â†’ Fixed, Retest â†’ Done. Makes testing work visible and manageable.

questions.scenarioText: A team consistently delivers working software each sprint but the business stakeholders say the product doesn't meet their needs. Stories are technically passing acceptance criteria but users find the product confusing.
questions.questionText: What type of testing is the team most likely neglecting?

options.text: Unit testing
Usability and user experience testing
Performance testing
Security testing

explanation.correct: If acceptance criteria pass but users find the product confusing, the team is missing usability/UX testing â€” verifying not just that it works, but that it's easy and intuitive to use. This lives in Agile Testing Quadrant Q3.
explanation.incorrect: Unit, performance, and security tests wouldn't address user confusion. Usability testing validates the user experience, which technical acceptance criteria often don't capture.
explanation.examTip: Q3 testing (business-facing, critique product): exploratory testing, usability testing, user acceptance testing. Often neglected in technical teams.

questions.questionText: What does the Agile principle 'working software over comprehensive documentation' mean for testers?

options.text: Testers should produce no test documentation in Agile projects
Test documentation should be sufficient to serve its purpose but not created for its own sake â€” focus on what adds value
Testers should focus on writing code instead of documentation
Test reports are not needed because working software proves quality

explanation.correct: Agile doesn't eliminate documentation â€” it eliminates unnecessary documentation. Testers should produce test charters, defect reports, automation results, and session notes where they add value, but avoid heavyweight test plans that nobody reads.
explanation.incorrect: No documentation is an extreme. Testers don't become coders. Test results are still needed for accountability and risk management.
explanation.examTip: Agile test documentation: produce what's needed for communication and risk management. Executable tests + defect logs + automated reports often suffice.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between a mock and a stub in test automation?

options.text: A mock and a stub are identical â€” both return pre-programmed responses
A stub provides pre-programmed responses to calls; a mock additionally verifies that specific interactions occurred as expected
A mock is for UI testing; a stub is for API testing
A stub is more advanced than a mock because it can simulate complex behaviours

explanation.correct: A stub returns pre-defined responses to calls (state-based testing). A mock also records interactions and verifies they happened correctly â€” e.g., verifying a specific method was called with specific parameters (behaviour-based testing).
explanation.incorrect: They are different test double types. Neither is limited by test layer. Mocks verify behaviour, stubs just provide data.
explanation.examTip: Test doubles: Dummy, Fake, Stub (canned responses), Spy (records calls), Mock (verifies interactions). From simplest to most complex.

questions.questionText: Why is it important for testers in Agile to have good communication and collaboration skills?

options.text: Because testers need to present defect reports to management
Because Agile testing is deeply integrated with development â€” testers must work closely with developers, PO, and business to ensure quality is everyone's responsibility
Because testers need to negotiate longer testing phases with project managers
Because communication skills are needed to write test case documentation

explanation.correct: In Agile, testers are embedded in the team and must continuously communicate with developers (defects, test findings), the PO (acceptance criteria, story questions), and business stakeholders â€” making communication skills as important as technical testing skills.
explanation.incorrect: Agile testers communicate with the whole team continuously, not just in formal reports or negotiations.
explanation.examTip: Agile tester mindset: collaborative, curious, communicative, technically skilled. Soft skills are as important as technical skills in Agile testing.

questions.questionText: Match each Agile Testing Quadrant to its correct description.

dropdowns.prompt: Technology-facing tests that support the team
Business-facing tests that critique the product (e.g., exploratory, usability)
Technology-facing tests that critique the product (e.g., performance, security)

explanation.correct: Q1=technology-facing/support team (unit, component tests). Q2=business-facing/support team (functional, story tests). Q3=business-facing/critique product (exploratory, usability). Q4=technology-facing/critique product (performance, security).
explanation.incorrect: The quadrants are defined by two axes: business vs technology facing, and support team vs critique product.
explanation.examTip: Agile Testing Quadrants axes: X=business vs technology facing; Y=support team vs critique product. All four quadrants are needed for complete test coverage.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of acceptance testing in an Agile sprint?

options.text: A formal phase after development where a separate QA team verifies the whole system
To verify that each user story meets its defined acceptance criteria within the sprint, confirming it delivers the expected business value
A contractual milestone where the customer formally accepts the software
The final test phase that occurs once per release before going to production

explanation.correct: In Agile, acceptance testing happens within each sprint for each story â€” verifying the story meets its acceptance criteria and delivering value to the PO. It's continuous, not a final phase.
explanation.incorrect: Acceptance testing in Agile is not a phase, formal contract milestone, or separate team activity â€” it's integrated into every sprint.
explanation.examTip: Agile acceptance testing: per story, within sprint, against acceptance criteria defined with the PO. Often automated using ATDD/BDD frameworks.

questions.questionText: In SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework), how is testing coordinated across multiple Agile teams?

options.text: Each team tests independently with no coordination
A centralised test team performs all testing for all Agile teams
Teams coordinate testing at the Program Increment (PI) level, including system integration testing across teams
Testing is deferred to a separate hardening sprint after all development is complete

explanation.correct: In SAFe, teams work in Program Increments (typically 8-12 weeks of 4 sprints + 1 IP sprint). System-level integration testing and cross-team dependencies are coordinated at the PI level through System Demos and IP sprints.
explanation.incorrect: Independent testing misses integration issues. Centralised test teams contradict Agile's whole-team quality. Deferring testing is an anti-pattern SAFe explicitly addresses.
explanation.examTip: SAFe testing: each team tests their own stories + system integration testing across teams. System Demo = combined increment demo. IP sprint = integration and hardening.

questions.questionText: What is the role of testers in Agile sprint retrospectives?

options.text: Testers present a list of all defects found in the sprint
